146.0.0.en: Alleluia. Praise the Lord, O my soul. While I live will I praise the Lord: I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being.

146.0.1.en: 1- The psalmist calls himself to praise before he calls others to it, for the one who has experienced praise and loves it has words that are effective when he calls others.

146.0.2.en: 2- The psalmist loved praise, so that he became accustomed to it, and came to praise throughout his life, as long as he is alive and present. And God supports him and encourages him, and encourages us all in the New Testament by His Holy Spirit continually.

146.0.3.en: Give yourself an opportunity to praise God in your prayer every day, by repeating a small portion of the Midnight Praise, or a psalm of thanksgiving, that you may taste a new sweetness in your sense of God during prayer.

146.1.0.en: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish.

146.1.1.en: 1- The psalmist makes clear the weakness of human beings, even if they are rulers and great men in the world, so that it is not possible to trust in them, because they are mortals subject to death and burial in the dust from which they were created.

146.1.2.en: 2- Jeremiah emphasizes not trusting in human beings, saying: "Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the Lord" (Jer 17:5-75), and likewise (Isa 31:

146.1.3.en: 1-3; 20:1-6.) For the material thoughts of a person, however great they may seem, can perish suddenly with the person's death, and the parable of the rich fool confirms the same meaning (Lk 12:16-21).

146.2.0.en: Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the Lord his God.

146.2.1.en: 1- It is understood from the two preceding verses that God is the only One in whom one can trust; He is the true Helper and Support, and the only hope of the people who believe in Him, and therefore we praise Him at all times. And whoever becomes accustomed to praising God learns to trust in Him and in no one else.

146.2.2.en: 2- The mention of the name of Jacob, who trusted in God, so that He blessed him and made him a great nation, which is the Jewish nation.

146.2.3.en: Do not be dazzled by the promises of people, and do not place your hope on words, for they are mortal human beings like you, but place your hope on God alone in everything.

146.3.0.en: Which made heaven, and earth, the sea, and all that therein is: which keepeth truth for ever. In this verse and the following verses the psalmist reviews the causes and reasons for trusting in the Lord, which are:

146.3.1.en: 1- "Which made heaven, and earth, the sea": and He is eternal and everlasting, and these creatures are very vast when compared with the small human being, and this calls a person to trust in the Creator of all creation.

146.3.2.en: 2- God's faithfulness in His promises, which continues throughout life and forever. But the promises of human beings are all shaky and not guaranteed, because they are subject to death, whereas God is constant, as proved by the fact that His vast creatures are constant, such as the heaven, the earth and the sea, and subject to the laws He set for them.

146.4.0.en: Which executeth judgment for the oppressed: which giveth food to the hungry. The Lord looseth the prisoners:

146.4.1.en: The psalm continues presenting the reasons for trusting in God, saying:

146.4.2.en: 3- "Which executeth judgment for the oppressed:" By the oppressed is of course meant the one who has endured hardships without any fault of his own, so God shows their right, even if after a while, and blesses them and compensates them. For this He shows His tenderness and calls us to trust in Him.

146.4.3.en: 4- "Which giveth food to the hungry:" For He feeds human beings and animals, even the smallest of them, namely the birds, and likewise the plants. He is a Father who feels for all His creatures, especially man, and above all this He cares for His children who trust in Him. And to His children who believe in Him He gives the greatest thing, which is spiritual food, that is, His Body and Blood, and nourishes them with His life-giving word.

146.4.4.en: 5- "The Lord looseth the prisoners:" By the prisoners is meant every person who is confined and humiliated, for when he cries out to God, He rescues him and looses him, as happened with Lot and all the prisoners whom Chedorlaomer the king took (Gen 14:17). The prisoners are also the prisoners of sin, whom Christ set free by His redemption on the Cross.

146.5.0.en: The Lord openeth the eyes of the blind: the Lord raiseth them that are bowed down: the Lord loveth the righteous:

146.5.1.en: The psalm adds new reasons for trusting in God, which are:

146.5.2.en: 6- "The Lord openeth the eyes of the blind:" God, who created the eyes, is able to heal them and give them light so that they see, as He opened the eyes of Tobit. But the matter is not limited to bodily eyes, but goes beyond them to spiritual eyes, for He grants insight and discernment to His children who trust in Him, such as the men of God in the Old Testament and the prophets. In the New Testament, Christ opened the eyes of many of the blind, and by the Holy Spirit gave enlightenment to the Apostles and the servants of the New Testament.

146.5.3.en: 7- "The Lord raiseth them that are bowed down:" that is, He makes them upright and straight and strong. Those who are bowed down are all who fell under heavy pressures that made them unable to do their work or to continue their lives, like Judith and her people, who were exposed to death by thirst. In the New Testament, Christ healed the woman who had been bowed down by the devil for eighteen years (Lk 13:13).

146.5.4.en: 8- "The Lord loveth the righteous:" they are the just who trust in Him, so He supported them and cared for them with His love, like the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And as Christ cared for His twelve disciples and the Apostles, and all His followers.

146.6.0.en: The Lord preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he turneth upside down.

146.6.1.en: And the psalm adds to the preceding reasons for trusting in God the following:

146.6.2.en: 9- "The Lord preserveth the strangers:" The stranger is the person who has no settled place and does not find his needs, so He cares for him and blesses him, as He preserved Abraham in Egypt (Gen 12:17), and blessed Isaac in Gerar (Gen 26:12), and Jacob in Egypt (Gen 47:27).

146.6.3.en: 10- "He relieveth the fatherless and widow": The fatherless is the one who has no father to care for him, and the widow is the one who has no husband to support her, so God took care of them, as He cared for the child Joash, whom Jehoiada the priest looked after and protected from the violence of Queen Athaliah until he sat on the throne (2 Kgs 11:17-21). And He blessed the widow of Zarephath of Sidon by Elijah's staying with her, and blessed the jar of oil and the barrel of meal throughout the famine (1 Kgs 17:14). And Christ had compassion on the widow of Nain and raised her son (Lk 7:11-15). And God cares for the fatherless and the widow in the spiritual sense, that is, those who have no strength or support, so God relieves them and supports them spiritually and in facing all the problems of life.

146.6.4.en: 11- "The way of the wicked he turneth upside down:" God does not allow the ways of the wicked to be always successful, so He protects the righteous from them, and if He overturns their ways He gives them an opportunity to repent and return to Him, when they see their failure, as He showed Pharaoh his weakness by the ten plagues in the days of Moses, and as He showed the weakness of the pagan kings in the days of the Judges, and freed His people from under their authority, and as Christ bound Satan on the Cross; for the way of the wicked is Satan, just as the way of the righteous is Christ.

146.7.0.en: The Lord shall reign for ever, even thy God, O Zion, unto all generations. Alleluia. God the Shepherd of His children, as appeared in the preceding verses, reigns over their hearts and cares for them; not only in this age, that is, this generation, but in the coming generation, which is eternal life. And all aspects of God's care for human beings were manifested in Christ in the New Testament, as we indicated in the preceding verses. Therefore the children of God are reassured and trust in Him, and He supports them throughout their lives and forever.

146.7.1.en: In all your needs take refuge in God and trust in Him, confident of His love, and you will live reassured and will not be disturbed by the changes of the people around you.

146.7.2.en: Praising God who cares for His people: "Praise ye the Lord: for it is good to sing praises unto our God" (v. 1). Introduction:

146.7.3.en: 1- Its author: unknown, since it has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms, but there are two other opinions:

146.7.4.en: a- David wrote it in the spirit of prophecy about the return from captivity and the building of Jerusalem and the temple.

146.7.5.en: b- In the Septuagint and Coptic versions it has the title "Ordained with Alleluia, for Haggai and Zechariah"

146.7.6.en: like the preceding psalm; that is, its author is Haggai or Zechariah.

146.7.7.en: 2- When was it written? There are two opinions:

146.7.8.en: a- In the days of David.

146.7.9.en: b- After the return from captivity.

146.7.10.en: 3- This psalm is one of the Hallel psalms, and it ends with the word Alleluia, and its beginning is the words "Praise ye", which resemble the word Alleluia.

146.7.11.en: 4- In the Septuagint, that is, the Agpeya, this psalm contains two psalms, Ps 146 and Ps 147; that is, this psalm in the Septuagint consists of two psalms, while in this Hebrew version it is one psalm.

146.7.12.en: 5- This psalm speaks about the return from captivity and the building of Jerusalem, which is a symbol of the Church of the New Testament.

146.7.13.en: 6- This psalm suits every penitent who feels that God has turned the ruin within him caused by sin into a great and joyful spiritual building; therefore he praises God.

146.7.14.en: 7- This psalm is liturgical, with the rest of the five Hallel psalms (Ps 146-150); it was prayed in the temple in the morning, and after the return from captivity, and likewise in the Jewish synagogues that were established about two centuries before the birth of Christ.

146.7.15.en: 8- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of Sleep, and it includes, as we said, the last two psalms, where the worshiper thanks God for His care of him, and the acceptance of his repentance and his restoration as a living member in the Church.

147.0.0.en: Praise ye the Lord: for it is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely.

147.0.1.en: 1- The psalmist calls the believers returning from captivity to Jerusalem to praise the Lord, because praising and singing psalms is good, for it lifts the soul to heavenly things and frees it from the bonds of earthly lusts.

147.0.2.en: 2- Praise is also pleasant to the soul ("pleasant"), making it rejoice and enjoy. And on the other hand, it is fitting for the soul that believes in God and loves Him to express its love by praise and singing. But the soul that does not praise proclaims its neglect of God and the weakness of its love, especially if God has done a great work with it, such as gathering the dispersed Jews who were captives and bringing them back to their land to build the temple of the Lord and worship Him in it; and of course praise and thanksgiving are required.

147.1.0.en: The Lord doth build up Jerusalem: he gathereth together the outcasts of Israel. He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.

147.1.1.en: 1- God's love appears in helping His children who returned from captivity to build their holy city Jerusalem. By this God gathered His people the children of Israel, who had been scattered in the lands of the world subject to Assyria and Babylon, and by this He heals the hearts of His people broken by humiliation and slavery, and binds up their broken souls, so that they are strengthened and become firm, and proudly glorify their God who rescued them and set them free, and favored them with the building of His temple and worship in it.

147.1.2.en: 2- Christ the Redeemer built the Church of His Body by His death on the Cross, and gathered the Jews and the Gentiles who believed in Him, and united them in faith in Him, and healed their souls broken by the humiliation of sin, so they lifted up their heads in joy and glorification of Him.

147.2.0.en: He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names. Great is our Lord, and of great power: his understanding is infinite.

147.2.1.en: 1- If God counts the vast and numberless stars and calls them by names, then His power is great and cannot be measured, nor can His understanding or knowledge be counted. If God is of such power and greatness, He is of course able to gather His scattered people and bring them back to Jerusalem and Judea to build the temple.

147.2.2.en: 2- The stars are the pious and the saints who were broken under slavery, and God bound up their souls and supported them, so they praised Him and became saints by the power of God.

147.2.3.en: 3- Christ is able to gather His children from the ends of the world, that they may believe in Him and become saints, that is, great stars, and to turn those who are far into those who are near, and opponents into apostles like Paul.

147.3.0.en: The Lord lifteth up the meek: he casteth the wicked down to the ground.

147.3.1.en: 1- The meek are the children of Israel who were captives, and God lifted them up by bringing them back from captivity at the command of Cyrus the emperor, king of Media and Persia, to build their city Jerusalem and its holy temple. As for the wicked, they are the Babylonians who humiliated the people of God, so He casts them down to the ground and humbles them by means of Media and Persia. The same thing happened with Pharaoh of Egypt and his army, who were shattered by the ten plagues and drowned in the Red Sea, while the people of God He freed from the slavery of Egypt, and took them through the midst of the Red Sea, and provided for them in the wilderness of Sinai.

147.3.2.en: 2- Christ humbled Himself and bound Satan the evil one, and raised up the Apostles, so they preached to the whole world, and cast down the opposing wicked, so they failed in resisting Christianity.

147.3.3.en: Thank God for the great works He has done with you throughout your life, and if you can, write them in a spiritual journal so that you do not forget them; all this establishes your faith and gladdens your heart.

147.4.s.en: (2) God's care for His pious ones

147.4.0.en: Sing unto the Lord with thanksgiving; sing praise upon the harp unto our God:

147.4.1.en: 1- After God favored His people with the return from captivity, it was natural for the psalm to call them to thank God, and even to accompany the thanksgiving with musical instruments, as an expression of intense joy and praise.

147.4.2.en: 2- Praise is the highest and loftiest degree of prayer, because it is pure love for God without any request. And whoever loves God speaks to Him with the words that He loves, which is praise.

147.5.0.en: Who covereth the heaven with clouds, who prepareth rain for the earth, who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains. He giveth to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry.

147.5.1.en: What moves us to praise God is His care for all His creatures, which appears in:

147.5.2.en: 1- "Who covereth the heaven with clouds:" God covers the high heavens with white cloud that gives a sense of mystery, yet God pours out rains from it upon the earth. So He covers the heavens with a beautiful sight, and satisfies man and the rest of creation by means of the rains.

147.5.3.en: And the cloud is a symbol of the saints, who are distinguished by spiritual radiance and pour out upon those around them an example and good teachings, as the rains come down from the cloud.

147.5.4.en: 2- "Who prepareth rain for the earth": God does not leave the earth dry, especially the land far from the rivers, but satisfies it, and man, and the animals, and the plants upon it, with the rains that come down from heaven.

147.5.5.en: And so all creatures serve man: the rains come from heaven, and the earth bears the plants and animals.

147.5.6.en: 3- "Who maketh grass to grow upon the mountains:" The mountains that appear dry and are hard to climb, when God sends rains upon them He makes grass grow on them, so their appearance becomes green and beautiful, and even sheep and cattle graze upon them, eat and are satisfied, and thank God. So the mountains that appear dry and barren God gives life, which is the grass, and the animals are fed. As God turns barren, parched souls into living, fruitful souls, which are even satisfied and serve those around them.

147.5.7.en: 4- "He giveth to the beast his food": The beasts cannot speak, but they express their hunger with sounds that God hears, so He hastens to feed them with various plants. And you, whenever you humble yourself, become like a beast before God, as the psalm said (Ps 73), not only materially but spiritually as well.

147.5.8.en: 5- "And to the young ravens which cry": God also feeds the young ravens that cry to Him, because when the raven's chicks come out of the eggs they are white, so he is afraid of them and their parents, the large ravens, are distressed, and fly far away and leave them. Then the chicks open their mouths and cry to God with weak voices, and He sends them large numbers of insects that are drawn toward the smell of their mouths, and they eat them, and the chicks grow, and the color of their feathers changes to black, so their parents the ravens become familiar with them and come to them to help them and care for them.

147.6.0.en: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man. The Lord taketh pleasure in his pious ones, in those that hope in his mercy.

147.6.1.en: God, whom we praise, rejoices in the humble who trust in Him and longs for their praise. He does not prefer the one who depends on the strength of military equipment, of which in ancient times the most important was the horse, and to it is added the bodily strength of the man, which appears in his legs able to run swiftly to attack and crush the enemies, but God takes pleasure in His pious ones who hope in His mercy with humility. For Satan calls human beings to depend on their strength and weapons and to leave God, and the remedy is the fear of God, forsaking sin, and humbling oneself before Him with many prayers, asking His mercy, and so we triumph over our enemies the demons however great their strength. For Solomon, who depended on the multitude of horses (2 Chr 9:25, 28), contrary to the Law (Deut 17:16), the kingdom was split after him; but Gideon, who feared God and depended on Him, triumphed over tens of thousands of enemies with three hundred men without weapons (Judg 7:7).

147.6.2.en: Do not be disturbed by the weakness of your resources, or the strength of those who attack you, because the power of God that is with you gives you victory over all the obstacles before you; walk in the fear of God and hope in His mercy, and you will receive all the blessings you need.

147.7.0.en: Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise thy God, O Zion. For he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates; he hath blessed thy children within thee. He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat. The bars of your gates: the posts of your gates, that is, the main boards of wood that make up the gates.

147.7.2.en: The finest of the wheat: the best kinds of wheat, full-bodied as if they were rich food.

147.7.3.en: 1- From (v. 12) Psalm 147 begins in the Septuagint, and it is the last psalm of the prayer of Sleep.

147.7.4.en: 2- For all the blessings mentioned above, the psalm calls Jerusalem, which is Zion, to praise the Lord her God, for He is a God special to her who loves her, because she is His holy city, and her inhabitants are His children, who worship Him in His great temple standing within Jerusalem.

147.7.5.en: 3- The reasons for Jerusalem's praise of God are many, the most important being:

147.7.6.en: a- "He hath strengthened the bars of thy gates:" meaning that He made your gates strong and fortified, so they protect the believers dwelling within Jerusalem. And this proclaims the power of God who protects His children.

147.7.7.en: And the door is Christ, as He Himself declared (Jn 10:7). And the gates are also a symbol of a person's senses, for God strengthens them so that they become pure and clean, and everything that enters the person is pure.

147.7.8.en: b- "He hath blessed thy children within thee:" in that He multiplies the believing children, and also sanctifies them and fills them with His power. And the children are also a symbol of a person's senses and virtues, for God blesses the senses and multiplies the virtues.

147.7.9.en: c- "He maketh peace in thy borders": that is, God keeps the boundaries of the lands belonging to Jerusalem, which is the region of Judea, so its inhabitants live in peace, and He drives the enemies away from them, so Jerusalem and those in it are able to love God and praise Him.

147.7.10.en: d- "Filleth thee with the finest of the wheat:" God gives her material blessings and satisfying food, granting her the best kinds of wheat, so she eats and is satisfied abundantly, and this is from the grace of God, and not because of the quality of the land or the weather conditions. And the finest of the wheat is a symbol of the Body and Blood of Christ, which is the best spiritual food.

147.8.0.en: He sendeth forth his commandment upon earth: his word runneth very swiftly.

147.8.1.en: 1- The word of God is His command to all His creation to serve man, and it is His commandments and His Law that were given to man to live by, and it is also His word on the lips of the prophets, and His living word in His pious men in the Old Testament, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

147.8.2.en: 2- The word of God is Christ incarnate in the fullness of time, who gave salvation to mankind, and it is the word of God on the lips of the Apostles, who preached to the whole world. And likewise the Fathers, the bishops, the priests and the servants in every generation.

147.9.0.en: He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes. He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold?

147.9.4.en: His cold: pointed slabs of ice that kill whoever they fall upon, as they fall in great numbers from a great height.

147.9.5.en: Other reasons the psalm presents for praising God, which are:

147.9.6.en: 1- "He giveth snow like wool:" His ability to turn nature to work contrary to its purpose. The extremely cold snow becomes like wool that warms the one who clings to it, as the children of Israel passed forty years with their simple clothes in the wilderness of Sinai, bitterly cold at night, where water turns to ice, yet God gave them warmth like those covered with wool. And this is a symbol that God turns spiritual coldness into a warm, even fervent, spiritual life.

147.9.7.en: 2- "He scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes:" The hoarfrost is cold, and ashes are the product of burning, that is, hot. And this is a symbol of God's turning spiritual coldness into repentance and contrition before God, so that sin is burned and becomes ashes, as the Holy Spirit burned sin within the believers when He came upon them, and burned in them every lust and sin by repentance.

147.9.8.en: 3- "He casteth forth his ice like morsels:" The ice is the hard snow broken into small pieces. And this is a symbol of the crushing of stony, hard hearts so that they become like crumbs. Indeed the morsels are also a symbol of crumbs of bread, that is, that they become useful to others, and become food and spiritual satisfaction for those around them, like Saul of Tarsus, hard of heart, who became Paul the Apostle and laid down his life for Christ, to satisfy the hungry souls among the Gentiles, and became a sensitive heart that feels for all his children, for he said: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).

147.9.9.en: 4- "Who can stand before his cold?" The cold represents God's justice and His punishment of the wicked, so whoever does not learn from all that has preceded and come to God, that is, persists in his evil, God's wrath comes upon him and destroys him. As happened with the pagan peoples who dwelt in the land of Canaan and whose evil increased, so God destroyed them (Josh 2:8), and as happened with Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen 19:28).

147.10.0.en: He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, and the waters flow.

147.10.1.en: 1- God is able by His word to command the creatures, so they act contrary to their nature; snow, hoarfrost, ice and cold are solids, but God is able to change them, so they turn into liquids that flow out upon people and animals, who drink from them, and it does not harm them but benefits them. As God changed the nature of the fire in the furnace with the three youths, so it did not harm them (Dan 3), and the ravenous lions became tame, gentle animals with Daniel (Dan 6:22), and the liquid water of the Red Sea became like a solid wall for the children of Israel to cross (Ex 14:22), whereas the dry ground under the feet of Dathan and Abiram became soft like the water of the sea, so they fell and the earth swallowed them (Num 16:31-33). And Aaron's dry rod became soft and blossomed and bore fruit (Num 17:8), and Balaam's ass, which cannot speak, spoke with wisdom better than the understanding of Balaam himself (Num 22:28).

147.10.2.en: 2- The word of God is Christ, who by His redemption and His Holy Spirit changes hard souls when they repent, so they become soft, obedient to the commandments of God, and even become servants who benefit and satisfy others.

147.11.0.en: He sheweth his word unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Israel. He hath not dealt so with any nation: and as for his judgments, they have not known them. Alleluia.

147.11.1.en: His statutes: the rites of worship.

147.11.2.en: His judgments: His commandments and His Law.

147.11.3.en: 1- God gave His people His word, that is, His commandments, and taught them His Law, that is, His judgments, and the ordinances of His worship in the temple, and taught them how to walk before Him through the fathers and the prophets, while all the world was pagan, sunk in ignorance and the worship of idols, immersed in their lusts, so God chose His people the children of Israel and taught them life with Him, that they might afterward be a light to the world.

147.11.4.en: 2- God also gave His incarnate Word, our Lord Jesus Christ, to be born in Jacob, that is, Bethlehem of Judea, and to preach to Israel, that is, all the Jewish people, the Law of the New Testament, which is the completion of the Law of the Old Testament, that they might live a lofty life in Christ, and then the Good News was spread by the Apostles to the whole world.

147.11.5.en: 3- The psalm began with the bringing back of His people Israel from captivity, to build the temple and worship Him. Then it addressed all human beings, and He lifted up the meek and rejected the wicked, and cared for all nature for the benefit of man, and after that it returned to speaking about His people Israel, showing that He gave them material blessings, and finally it speaks about His spiritual blessings that He granted to His people. All this so that His people might be a light to all the world.

147.11.6.en: For God loves His people, and loves all human beings, because they are His children.

147.11.7.en: Reflect on the material blessings God has given you, and thank Him for them. And may you write them down, then reflect on His spiritual blessings, and write them down as well, and lift up your heart in praise, that your heart may rise to God and be lifted above sin and passing lusts.

147.11.8.en: The whole world praises God: "Alleluia. Praise ye the Lord from the heavens: praise him in the heights" (v. 1). Introduction:

147.11.9.en: 1- Its author: unknown, because the psalm has no title, so it is one of the orphan psalms.

147.11.10.en: 2- This psalm begins and ends with the word Alleluia, so it is one of the five Hallel psalms (Ps 146-150).

147.11.11.en: 3- This psalm is liturgical among the Jews, and it was prayed in common worship.

147.11.12.en: 4- This psalm is one of the important liturgical psalms in the Church. It is the first part of the Fourth Hoos, that is, the fourth praise, which is prayed before the evening prayer (Eshiya), or at the end of the Midnight Praise.

147.11.13.en: 5- This psalm is considered one of the greatest psalms of praise, because it gathers all creation in one praise to God.

147.11.14.en: 6- This psalm suits every worshiper who loves God and wants to express his feelings to Him, and as a leader of creation in praising God.

147.11.15.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
